Dodge Is Back In NASCAR And All Is Well With The World
sum: There was so much news this week that I had to wait until Friday to write about the one story I personally cared about in The Morning Dump: Dodge is back in the top-level NASCAR Cup series. Yes, yes, yes, yes. America is so back, baby!

Other, less interesting people might argue that the news that former VW North America chief Pablo Di Si is getting the COO job here is the bigger Stellantis news, but nope, it’s the NASCAR thing. Oh, hey, remember when Audi announced a plant in Georgia, and it got all caught up in politics? Now that the elections are behind us, Audi is apparently looking to expand even more there than initially announced.
Remember Hertz? Hertz still exists, but it’s not going super well. Maybe they should rent V8-powered 911s? Those are fun.
Dodge And NASCAR Go Together Like Peanut Butter And Chocolate, Or A PB Cup And My Belly

The last year that Dodge ran in the top-level Cup series was in 2012, which was also the final outing of the 5th generation cars. They went out on top, with Brad Keselowski winning the championship. The then-Italian-American brand disinvested from NASCAR as it focused on other things. When FCA became Stellantis, it seemed even more remote that Dodge would return.

That all changed when the American arm of the company took over last year, and we were all treated to RAM running in the NASCAR truck series (you can watch our own Parker Kligerman racing tonight in a RAM). Rightly, everyone saw this as a prelude to the return of Dodge and its Charger to Cup.

Tim Kuniskis, head of American Brands, SRT Performance and Direct Connection division, Stellantis North America, shared the news during a sneak preview of the Stellantis display at the 2026 Specialty Equipment Market Association (SEMA) Show. For Dodge, the message is simple: gasoline-powered performance is back at the center of the brand, and Dodge is heading back to NASCAR Cup Series racing.

Stocks Plunge on an AI Selloff and Tesla Falls More Than 8%. What It Means for Car Buyers and Automakers
sum: Stocks sold off sharply Thursday as AI and chip stocks led Wall Street lower and erased the post-election rally. Intraday, the Nasdaq fell about 5%, the S&P 500 roughly 3% to 4% and the Dow more than 1,100 points, according to Yahoo Finance and Bloomberg. Tesla opened down more than 8%. The auto industry was already working through weaker consumer confidence and higher borrowing costs, so the question is how much a market slide adds.

Tesla trades more like a growth and tech stock than a traditional automaker, which is why it moves with the Nasdaq. Ford, GM and Stellantis have faced their own pressure. Stellantis shares fell 7% on Oct. 2 and 8% on Oct. 23 in separate sessions, and Ford and Stellantis each dropped about 4% in August after the White House set 50% auto tariffs on Canada.

Cox Automotive’s updated October estimate put the seasonally adjusted sales rate at 15.5 million, below its 16.1 million forecast. Volume came in around 1.324 million units, up 2.9% from a year earlier but under forecast. Cox cited weak stock market performance, election uncertainty, poor consumer confidence and rising loan rates, and said retail demand accounted for most of the shortfall because fleet sales rose nearly 6%. Cox also credited wealthier buyers and wider access to credit with keeping the market stronger than low confidence alone would suggest, and wealthier buyers are the group a falling stock market is most likely to affect.

The Manheim Used Vehicle Value Index stood at 207.4 in mid-October, up 0.7% from September on an adjusted basis and up 2.2% from a year earlier. Cox’s Jonathan Gregory said “supply, not demand, appears to be what slowed depreciation,” and described dealer demand as roughly flat. If buyers pull back further, flat demand leaves wholesale prices with little cushion.

Falling stock prices alone rarely change a car payment. Loan rates matter more, and the 10-year Treasury yield eased to about 4.84% from 4.90% on Thursday, according to Bloomberg. Buyers with a strong trade-in or cash may gain leverage if automakers add incentives to move retail inventory, though that usually takes weeks to show up. Buyers financing most of a purchase should watch rates and lender standards more than headlines.

items.t: Stellantis Earnings Cheer Lifts Shares 15%; Stoxx Europe 600 Posts Third Straight Gain as Spanish Stocks Lag
sum: European stocks closed mixed on Wednesday (the 28th), as divergent third-quarter corporate earnings, a rebound in international oil prices of more than 1.7%, and the impending European Central Bank (ECB) rate decision kept trading sentiment cautious. The pan-European Stoxx Europe 600 index ended up 0.46 points, or 0.07%, at 644.14 points, marking a third consecutive session of gains after bulls and bears battled through the session and the index barely held above the flat line.

Among major regional markets, Germany's Frankfurt DAX index rose 0.44% to 25,704.02 points; the UK's FTSE 100 edged up 0.07% to 10,694.50 points; Italy's FTSE MIB gained 0.40% to 49,824.30 points; and France's CAC 40 slipped 0.18 points to 7,886.96 points. Spain's IBEX 35 index, weighed down by heavy selling in bank stocks, fell 1.45% to 18,883.50 points, the weakest performer among the five major markets.
The table below shows the closing performance of major European stock markets on the 28th:
Note: France's CAC 40 fell only marginally by 0.18 points on the day, a decline of less than 0.01%.

By sector, autos rose 1.33%, ranking as the center of buying interest among the 20 major sectors, driven mainly by multinational auto giant Stellantis. The company reported third-quarter revenue up 1% year-on-year to €37.6 billion (approximately $41.9 billion), with adjusted operating profit climbing sharply from €90 million (approximately $100.3 million) in the year-earlier period to €256 million (approximately $285.2 million), while net losses narrowed significantly. After the results were released, Stellantis shares surged more than 15% in a single session, becoming the key force propping up the broader European market.

Bank stocks diverged markedly. Deutsche Bank shares jumped about 4% after its third-quarter profit beat market expectations; Standard Chartered closed up 2.4% after raising its full-year growth and profit targets. By contrast, Spain's Banco Santander plunged 5.6%, dragged down by weak profitability in its Brazilian operations, becoming the main culprit weighing on the Spanish stock market.

Stellantis shares extend their decline, down 63% year to date
sum: Stellantis ended another negative session on Wall Street on October 23, with STLA shares closing at $4.06, down 4.92%. The stock recovered part of its losses after falling as low as $3.92 during the session, but the picture since the start of 2026 remains bleak, with shares in the Antonio Filosa-led group down 62.7%.
Stellantis stock extends its decline as 2026 losses approach 63%

Compared with the U.S. intraday record high of $29.51 reached on March 25, 2024, the current price represents a decline of around 86.2%. In just over two and a half years, the stock has therefore fallen to less than one-seventh of the level it reached during that session.

Analyst downgrades and wider concerns about the automotive sector weighed on the latest trading day. HSBC cut its price target for Stellantis’ European shares from €4 to €3.30 while maintaining its Reduce rating. Volvo’s losses also sent the Swedish company’s stock down nearly 30%, adding pressure to shares of other automakers.

The weakness accumulated throughout the year comes as Stellantis works through a costly industrial overhaul. In February, the company announced €22.2 billion in charges related to the second half of 2025, covering changes to vehicle programs, the battery supply chain and warranty estimates. Filosa acknowledged that the company had previously overestimated the pace of electric vehicle adoption.

Around €6.5 billion of those charges will require cash payments over four years. Stellantis’ 2025 loss also led the company to suspend its dividend in 2026, leaving shareholders without a payout on top of the decline in the stock price.

Subsequent financial results showed improvement, although margins remained thin. Second-quarter revenue rose 13% to €43.5 billion, while net profit reached €293 million. Adjusted operating income margin stood at 1.8%, with Enlarged Europe still posting a loss on that measure.

items.t: FTSE MIB Falls to 49,086 as Banks, Insurers and Stellantis Lead Milan Lower
sum: Piazza Affari was the worst-performing major market in Europe on Monday 19 October 2026 as French political turmoil revived euro-area sovereign risk, the BTP-Bund spread widened to its highest since 9 October and Italy's heavily weighted financial sector sold off.

The FTSE MIB closed at 49,086 points on Monday 19 October 2026, down 1.55% on the session, according to Borsa Italiana closing data reported by ANSA and SoldiOnline. The index traded in a range between a low of 48,836 and a high of 49,592, and it slipped below the 49,000 mark around 15:30 CEST before buyers lifted it back above that threshold into the close. The broader FTSE Italia All Share fell 1.51%, the FTSE Italia Mid Cap lost 0.94% and the FTSE Italia Star index of smaller high-quality companies declined 0.76%.

Trading activity thinned slightly, with the value of shares exchanged falling to 2.74 billion euros from 3.1 billion euros on Friday. Monday's drop made Milan the weakest of the four major western European benchmarks: the CAC 40 lost 1.11%, the DAX 40 fell 1.18% and the FTSE 100 declined 1.08%. The FTSE MIB had been the session's worst performer in the European Union as early as midday, according to Milano Finanza's live coverage.

Italy's market is dominated by banks and insurers, and that structure made it especially vulnerable to the main theme of the day: a renewed flare-up in euro-area sovereign risk triggered by events in France. Weekend riots linked to cost-of-living protests, with around 1,800 arrests and Limoges' town hall set alight, pushed the French 10-year OAT yield up to 4.92% and widened its spread over Bunds to 1.47 points. Investors quickly extended that concern to other high-debt euro-area countries.

In Italy, the BTP-Bund spread widened to as much as 110.8 basis points, its highest level since 9 October, according to Milano Finanza, at the same time as the Treasury was placing a new BTP Valore retail bond. A wider spread raises funding costs for the state and reduces the market value of the government bonds that Italian banks hold in large quantities, so lender shares tend to fall when the spread moves higher. Milano Finanza's 11:35 update linked the two directly, flagging rising French risk alongside a 4% drop in Stellantis.

sum: Stellantis shares moved higher again on the morning of September 28 recording a 2.32% gain in Paris at 9:50 a.m. The rebound follows a difficult period for the automaker’s stock and came alongside a positive start in Milan, where Stellantis ranked among the session’s stronger performers.

The market move comes as Antonio Filosa continues to reorganize the company and works to improve financial performance while rebuilding the North American business. That effort also includes decisions about which plants will build future models, choices that directly affect labor relations and production plans for the coming years.

In Canada, for example, the future of the Brampton plant continues to complicate contract negotiations with Unifor. In its September 24 update, the union challenged the possible sale of the factory to armored-vehicle manufacturer Roshel and Stellantis’ decision to link that issue with an agreement covering its other Canadian operations. The negotiations involve more than 9,000 Stellantis employees across the country.

Stellantis also outperformed the broader European markets during the morning. A 9:20 a.m. market update showed Paris up around 0.4% and Milan essentially flat, while Stellantis had gained 2.24% in Milan. Those figures come from different exchanges and slightly different times than the 2.32% increase in Paris, but both showed a strong start for the automaker’s shares.

Technical analysis identifies €4.154 as the first resistance level, an area where stronger selling pressure could slow the advance. A move above that threshold could strengthen the case for a continued short-term recovery, although it would not by itself confirm a broader change in trend.

On the downside, the analysis places the first support at €4.083, a level traders can watch to gauge whether buying interest can limit another decline. A drop below that area could open the way toward €4.046 under the technical scenario. These figures serve as reference points based on recent price action rather than levels the stock will necessarily reach.
Stellantis still trails the CAC 40 on a weekly basis, showing that Monday morning’s gain has not erased its recent relative weakness against the French market.

sum: Four automakers with nothing in common are surging in lockstep Thursday morning, and the reason behind that unusual uniformity tells investors something important about whether the gains will stick.

Automaker stocks are moving together in Thursday morning trading, and the uniformity of the bid says more about the day than any single release. General Motors (NYSE:GM | GM Price Prediction) is leading a Detroit-and-Tesla group higher on rotation into cyclicals, with no earnings, guidance change, recall or sales report attached to the move. General Motors stock is up 4% to $87.33, leading a group whose members would ordinarily trade on their own news.

The scale of the bid registers first at the fund level. The Consumer Discretionary Select Sector SPDR ETF (NYSEARCA:XLY) is up 1.4% to $111.69, a category running ahead of the broad tape. Meanwhile, the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSEARCA:SPY) is up 1.1% to $762.37, with General Motors and its automaker peers rising faster than either fund.

Turning to major U.S. automakers, Stellantis N.V. (NYSE:STLA) stock is up 4% to $5.09, running alongside General Motors on the same rotation flow. Ford Motor (NYSE:F) stock is up 3% to $13.73, keeping pace with General Motors despite a very different balance sheet. At the same time, Tesla (NASDAQ:TSLA) stock is up 2% to $366.37, joining the same bid despite a business mix that shares little with General Motors beyond a listed vehicle.

No automaker released material information this morning. There’s no earnings report scheduled, no guidance revision, no recall notice and no monthly sales tally to hang the move on. The pattern across General Motors and its peers is money entering a category, not a reaction to disclosure.

The tell is uniformity. Four automakers with very different geographies, product mixes and recent operating records are moving within a narrow band on the same session, and General Motors is leading a group whose members would ordinarily diverge on their own tapes. Company-specific catalysts move one name at a time; this is a bid on the label.
That General Motors sits at the top is consistent with rotation favoring the name with the strongest recent operating record. It isn’t evidence of anything General Motors disclosed today.

sum: Traders on the Milan Stock Exchange popped the champagne just long enough to send Stellantis shares ticking up 1.71% following August’s Italian vehicle registration report. On paper, the figures look like a victory lap. The automotive giant posted a 6.2% surge in Italian registrations last month, nearly double the overall market’s modest 3.15% bump, lifting its domestic market share from 26.4% to 27.2%.

Zooming out to the first eight months of 2026, the victory lap gets even louder. Stellantis registered 341,225 vehicles in Italy between January and August, jumping 14% compared to the 299,264 units logged over the same stretch in 2025. That easily beat the broader Italian market’s 8.54% expansion, bumping Stellantis’s eight-month market share up to 30.2% from 28.7%.

Across major European markets, group registrations climbed 7% against a 5% industry benchmark, prompting casual observers to assume executive management was orchestrating an operational masterclass. Then the analysts at Intermonte ruined the party by reading the fine print.
Strip out the contributions from Chinese joint-venture partner Leapmotor, and Stellantis’s European growth suddenly collapses to an underwhelming 3.5%, sliding right behind the market average.

To make matters spicier, the sales mix looks like a balance-sheet headache. While passenger car registrations rose 11%, lucrative light commercial vehicles dropped 5%. Growth wasn’t driven by high-margin luxury nameplates either. Cheap Fiats and budget Citroëns carried the volume, while higher-value brands actively dragged down the spreadsheet.

As Equita dryly observed, Stellantis underperformed in France, and its Italian bragging rights depend entirely on counting Leapmotor’s imported hardware. Over in North America, the group managed to beat the market almost exclusively because Ram trucks continue to shoulder the load.

Yet despite the margin-squeezing product mix and mounting European geopolitical headwinds, analysts at Sim remain remarkably optimistic. They expect dealer shipments (sell-in) to outpace customer registrations in the third quarter as new models roll out, maintaining that Stellantis can still hit its mid-single-digit revenue growth targets for 2026.

sum: The delay of new US tariffs on Canadian goods triggered a strong rebound in automotive stocks, allowing Stellantis shares to gain around 6% and climb back to €4.63. Trading volume nearly doubled the average recorded during the previous month after the group’s shares had fallen to their lowest level since 2016 and lost roughly 46% over the past year. Stellantis shares surge 6%, but investors remain cautious about the turnaround

Washington delayed the introduction of additional 50% tariffs on roughly $20 billion worth of Canadian imports for three days. Donald Trump described the move as the result of a last-minute agreement that still requires final documentation, while Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney confirmed substantial progress without declaring the negotiations complete. The short extension temporarily avoids another escalation and gives both governments more time to discuss measures that also affect automotive trade.

Stellantis was not the only automaker to benefit from the news. General Motors and Ford both gained more than 2%, suggesting that investors mainly reacted to the immediate reduction in trade pressure across the North American auto industry. Manufacturers and suppliers on both sides of the US-Canada border depend heavily on the constant movement of vehicles, components and raw materials between the two countries.

Stellantis remains particularly exposed to these tensions. In its second-quarter results, the group estimated that tariffs could have a net impact of €1 billion to €1.2 billion in 2026, after recording €300 million during the first half of the year. That six-month figure also includes a €400 million tariff reimbursement, which reduced the effective cost reported during the period.
Interest from US dealers in the Fiat Topolino also emerged during the same period.

The beleaguered automaker has a $70 billion turnaround strategy it is calling "FaSTLAne 2030." The different levels within the automotive industry can be a little tricky with wording, so let's sort that out. Shipments are not the same as sales. Rather, shipments count the vehicles delivered to dealers and distribution companies, while sales track the number of vehicles actually purchased by end consumers.

Stellantis' second-quarter 2026 results give us a prime example of why the distinction between shipments and sales matters. Stellantis' global shipments increased by 10% year over year during the second quarter to 1.6 million. That increase was driven in large part by a 38% surge right here in North America.
In contrast, Stellantis' North American sales rose only 5.7% during the second quarter, well below the 38% surge in shipments to dealers. This suggests a buildup of inventory on dealership lots.

sum: Most of us enjoy a good comeback story, and that's exactly what Stellantis (NYSE: STLA) hopes to achieve by the end of this decade. The struggling carmaker is putting its money where its mouth is with a $70 billion turnaround strategy that focuses not just on North America, but Europe as well, through a multipronged approach to affordable pricing as the price of new vehicles continues to rise.

Stellantis is committed to driving 70% of its investment through four core brands: Jeep, Ram, Peugeot, and Fiat. If the automaker executes its strategy well, investors should be well rewarded with market-beating returns through the rest of this decade. Lost in the shuffle, though, is a key resurgence in Europe. Let's dive in.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

It appears that Jeep will be instrumental in reversing Stellantis' fortunes in Europe. Investors know SUVs are big business in the U.S. market, but many don't realize that small SUVs and crossovers are Europe's second-largest segment, and compact SUVs and crossovers remain the largest segment.

The turnaround could be considered low-hanging fruit for the automaker, as about five years ago, strict European emissions standards reduced its product lineup to only two SUVs. Jeep stopped importing its Grand Cherokee and Gladiator pickup back in 2024; imports of the Wrangler ended last year because those gasoline-powered vehicles would have bumped its corporate average CO2 emissions too high in the near term.

The game plan is roughly this: Stellantis will import the Jeep Recon electric midsize SUV in 2027, after it launches in North America this year. That will be followed by another Jeep import developed with Chinese partner, Dongfeng, in 2028. Two more small Jeep SUVs will then be produced in Europe on the STLA One platform between 2028 and 2030, which aims to cut production costs by 20% compared to current platforms.
